commitResults.messageTitle: Add support for storing and listing tasks
Add support for todo, deadline, and event tasks
Handle empty todo description and unknown commands
Use a CommandType enum for command dispatch (A-Enums)
Save tasks to disk when list changes
Load tasks from disk on startup

commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline stores its "by" field as a plain String and prints
or saves it back exactly as the user typed it.

An arbitrary string like "June 6th" or "asap" is accepted
just as readily as a real date, so the chatbot can't
validate, compare, or reformat deadlines in any meaningful
way.

Let's parse the /by argument into a java.time.LocalDate at
input time, keep that as the stored representation, and
format it separately for display and for the save file.

LocalDate gives parsing and validation for free, rejects a
malformed date before it's ever stored, and gives later
features (like filtering tasks by date) something concrete
to compare against.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add on command to find tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
There's no way to see which tasks fall on a specific date;
the only option is to list everything and read through it
by hand.

As the list grows this gets tedious, and the LocalDate field
added to Deadline is otherwise write-only from the user's
point of view.

Let's add an "on DATE" command that filters tasks down to
whichever ones report a match via a new isOccurringOn()
method, defined on Task (default false) and overridden in
Deadline.

Checking task.isOccurringOn(date) keeps the filtering logic
on Task/Deadline rather than scattering instanceof checks
through Elora, and leaves room to extend the same capability
to Event later without touching the command-handling code.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui, Storage, Parser, TaskList classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Elora.java is one class holding roughly 330 lines: command
dispatch, every System.out.println call, and raw file
reading/writing, all mixed together in a single loop.

This makes each concern hard to test or reuse in isolation,
and any change - a wording tweak, a save-format tweak, a new
command - forces touching the same large method regardless of
which concern it actually belongs to.

Let's extract Ui (all reading and printing), Storage (loading
and saving the data file), Parser (turning raw input into a
command word, arguments, and a CommandType), and TaskList (the
task collection and its operations), leaving Elora to hold one
of each and orchestrate them in run().

Each class now has exactly one reason to change, and the
split follows the seams already visible in the old code -
println calls, file I/O calls, string-parsing calls, and
list-manipulation calls were each already grouped together,
just not separated into their own files.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into elora and elora.task packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All eleven classes sit in the default (unnamed) package,
directly under src/main/java, with no package declarations.

The Java coding standard requires every class to belong to a
named package, and grouping unrelated classes in the default
package doesn't scale as the codebase grows.

Let's split the classes into two packages: elora for the app
machinery (Elora, Ui, Storage, Parser, CommandType,
EloraException) and elora.task for the task domain model
(Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList), moving each file with
git mv and adding the matching package declaration plus any
cross-package imports needed.

This groups task-related classes together, separate from what
drives the app itself, satisfies both the Minimal and Stretch
goal bars in one pass, and follows the same seam the A-MoreOOP
refactor already established.

build.gradle's application block still points mainClass at
seedu.duke.Duke, left over from the add-gradle-support branch
being created before the chatbot was renamed and repackaged.

With that stale value, ./gradlew run can't find the class and
fails to launch the application.

Let's update mainClass to elora.Elora, matching where the
entry point actually lives now.

This is the only change needed for Gradle's run task to work
- everything else in build.gradle (Java version, dependencies,
standard-input wiring) is already correct for this project.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser, Task, TaskList, Deadline
commitResults.messageBody:
The codebase has no automated tests; every method has only
been checked by hand-running the chatbot and reading its
console output.

Manual checking doesn't scale, and it's easy to silently
break an already-working method - a date-parsing edge case, an
off-by-one in TaskList - while changing something nearby
without ever noticing.

Let's add JUnit 5 tests for the classes with pure, side-effect-
free logic - Parser, Task, TaskList, and Deadline - covering
the command-parsing branches, done/not-done state transitions,
list add/remove/date-filtering, and Deadline's date formatting
and comparison.

These four classes hold most of the project's actual decision-
making logic and have no file or console I/O to work around,
making them the highest-value targets for JUnit. Ui, Storage,
and Elora are left for a later pass, since testing them
meaningfully needs mocked I/O or a temp filesystem rather than
straightforward method calls.

build.gradle's shadowJar task still names its output
duke.jar, left over from the add-gradle-support branch, from
before the chatbot was renamed.

Distributing a JAR called duke.jar for a chatbot named Elora
is confusing for anyone who downloads it from a release.

Let's rename shadowJar's archiveFileName to elora.jar,
matching the application's actual name.

This is a cosmetic rename only - the shadowJar task, mainClass,
and everything else needed to produce a working fat JAR were
already configured correctly during A-Gradle.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Javadoc to elora package classes
commitResults.messageBody:
None of the classes in the elora package have header comments;
a reader has to open each method body to learn what it does.

The coding standard requires header comments on public classes
and methods, and undocumented public methods force every caller
to read the implementation just to know what a method expects
or returns.

Let's add Javadoc to every class and public method in the elora
package (Elora, Ui, Storage, Parser, CommandType,
EloraException), following the format the standard specifies:
a summary sentence, a blank line, then @param/@return where
they add real value.

Simple getters and straightforward @Override methods are left
undocumented, consistent with the standard's own exemptions for
those two cases.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Javadoc to elora.task package classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, and TaskList have no header
comments either.

Same reason as the elora package: undocumented public methods
force readers into the implementation, and the coding standard
requires these comments.

Let's add the same treatment to the task-domain classes,
including describing each subclass's specific
toString()/toSaveFormat() format, since those differ
meaningfully from Task's base version rather than being an
exact override.

Kept as its own commit, separate from the elora package
changes, so each commit stays focused on one package - matching
the file organization A-Packages already established.

commitResults.messageTitle: Resolve leftover conflict markers in Storage.java
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage.java still contained unresolved <<<<<<< / ======= /
>>>>>>> conflict markers from an earlier merge, committed as
literal text instead of being resolved.

Literal conflict markers aren't valid Java, so the project
fails to compile.

Let's replace the file with its correct, fully-merged content -
the Javadoc from A-JavaDoc plus the line-wrap from
A-CodingStandard, with nothing left over from either side's
markers.

Verified by recompiling the whole project and re-running the
full regression test after this fix.
